title: Have we seen an acceleration in cyberattacks?
text:
This week’s cybersecurity events have been cause for alarm: PHP2Shell vulnerabilities have triggered widespread patching and precautionary shutdowns, and AI agents have been documented in attacks against banks, healthcare organizations, and corporate cloud systems.
At the same time, AI models, including open-weight ones, continue to scale their cyber capability. Vals AI reports that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, a Chinese open-weight model, outperformed the frontier closed model GPT 6 Sol on its multi-step offensive cybersecurity evaluation at substantially lower cost.
These developments raise a broader question: is there evidence of a measurable acceleration in cyberattacks in 2026?
Following Cunningham & Rush (2026), we examine publicly available data on cryptocurrency hacks and ransomware for signs of acceleration. Our preliminary findings are:


Recorded cryptocurrency hacks accelerated after April 2026.1
The increase was particularly pronounced for crypto code exploits and smaller thefts. We also find acceleration among larger thefts, though it is less pronounced.
Recorded ransomware attacks show no clear acceleration, but growth in the number of ransomware hacker groups posting victims has accelerated.
Ransomware hacker groups are sending more AI-generated negotiation messages, though these remain a small share of all negotiation messages.


Additionally, Appendix A checks the crypto findings against six other hack trackers.
Overall, we are moderately confident (~75%) that crypto attacks have accelerated in 2026.2 We open-source our code, data, and results in our GitHub repo.

title: Have we seen an acceleration in cyberattacks?
text:
Crypto attacks

Data source. Our main source is DeFiLlama, a public crypto-data website that keeps a list of hacks on decentralized finance. We downloaded a dataset of 1,306 incidents from 2011 to 2026 (of which 1,218 are from 2020-2026), each with a date, an amount stolen, and a classification of the cause. We have also collected data from other websites that recorded crypto attacks, including CertiK, Comparitech, and more, in Appendix A.



Tentative Finding 1: The number of recorded crypto hacks has accelerated in 2026







Tentative Finding 2: Most of that acceleration comes from smaller thefts in 2026
The increase in recorded small thefts could reflect two mechanisms:

Cheaper attacks: AI lowers the cost of carrying out an attack, which makes smaller targets worth the effort.
Better detection: AI helps discover anomalies, increasing the rate of identification of smaller thefts that would previously have gone unnoticed or unreported.

We cannot distinguish these mechanisms. We assign a subjective probability of 75% that both are contributing, with some real rise in cheaper attacks.







Tentative Finding 3: Total losses show little acceleration




Note: DeFiLlama gives no dollar loss for 37 of the 1,218 hacks listed since January 2020 (3%). By year, the share ranges from 0.5% (2023) to 5.1% (2024), and it is 3.4% in 2026. This chart counts those hacks as zero, so monthly totals are slightly understated.





Tentative Finding 4: The amount of loss from each exploit did not accelerate in 2026




Note: DeFiLlama gives no dollar loss for 37 of the 1,218 hacks listed since January 2020 (3%). By year, the share ranges from 0.5% (2023) to 5.1% (2024), and it is 3.4% in 2026. This chart averages only the hacks with a dollar loss.





Tentative Finding 5: Accelerations in hacking vary by exploit type
We counted DeFiLlama hacks by month and exploit type across 13 categories from January 2023 to September 2026, excluding incomplete October data.
Many of our findings fit what we’d intuitively expect.

Many accelerated exploit types (input validation, access control, token and share accounting, oracle manipulation, key compromise) involve finding software flaws or reasoning about how a protocol behaves. These are tasks that AI coding agents could plausibly accelerate.
Many non-accelerated exploit types (rug pulls, social engineering, market manipulation, governance) principally depend on persuading people, building credibility, or attracting investor funds. So, these hacks are probably less accelerated by improved AI coding capabilities.

The pattern is not clear-cut, though: reentrancy is also a code-based exploit category, yet it did not show acceleration in our analysis.
One possible explanation is that AI tools reduce the effort required for some exploit types more than others. Another possible explanation is that AI tools help discover anomalies that are also more AI-exploitable. The second explanation may be a little far-fetched in our opinion, because AI-assisted detection and AI-exploitability do not necessarily go hand in hand. For example, machine-learning methods can effectively detect rug pulls, even though rug pulls themselves don’t seem to be particularly AI-exploitable.







Caveat: Overall, we are ~75% confident that 2026 displays a genuine acceleration in the number of crypto hacks, beyond changes in detection and reporting.
The increase in recorded hacks could partly reflect improved detection, reporting, or database coverage. We could not verify whether DeFiLlama’s collection process remained consistent over the study period, so we cannot rule out that changes stemmed from the discovery of incidents. We therefore compare the pattern across other trackers (see Appendix A), although agreement across trackers would not fully resolve this concern if they rely on overlapping reports or detection systems.
To help address this concern, we also examine attacks involving losses of at least $1 million, since larger thefts are harder to miss. We find an acceleration in larger attacks too, though the acceleration is much smaller.
We also break down attacks by exploit type. The categories showing acceleration tend to be the ones that we’d expect to be more amenable to AI assistance. It is also possible that these exploits might also be easier to discover using AI, leaving the same underlying uncertainty.
A related article by DeFiLlama and Firepan examines whether the share of hacks reproducible using AI has increased. However, it compares 2020-2021 with 2024-2026, making it difficult to determine whether there was an acceleration specifically in 2026.
We will update this estimate as more evidence becomes available.

title: Have we seen an acceleration in cyberattacks?
text:
Ransomware attacks
We also examined ransomware attacks using two sources. Ransomware.live records victims named on ransomware gangs’ “leak sites,” websites where gangs threaten to publish stolen data to pressure victims into paying. Comparitech’s Ransomware Intelligence Platform includes only attacks confirmed by another source, such as a victim statement, a data-breach notice, or a news report.


Tentative Finding 1: The number of victims listed on ransomware leak sites has shown little acceleration.







Tentative Finding 2: The number of recorded independently confirmed attacks has not accelerated.
This difference could partly reflect delays in disclosure. US state laws require organizations to notify affected individuals of certain data breaches, so disclosure is not always voluntary. However, these notices can take months after an incident to appear. So, the counts for recent quarters may rise as more attacks are disclosed and added to the dataset.







Tentative Finding 3: There is a slight acceleration in the number of hacker groups posting ransomware victims.







Tentative Finding 4: Evidence of AI use in ransomware negotiations
We used Pangram 4.1 to examine possible AI use in publicly available ransomware negotiations from the Ransomchat dataset. The dataset contained 276 chats and 12,889 messages involving 31 ransomware hacker groups. We selected timestamped, English-language attacker messages longer than 50 words and excluded templates, which left us with 344 messages.
Note that our 2026 results are mostly limited to Q1: Ransomchat updates its dataset with a lag, which means that it has little coverage of Q2-Q3 2026. The 21 September 2026 Ransomchat snapshot contained few negotiations after March 2026, and historically, for chats since 2023, the median publication lag was four months, and the mean was five months.
Also note that the 2021 data point is likely a false positive.







Hacker data:
Some ransomware hackers appear to have started drafting negotiation messages with LLMs in 2025-26. Examples:
Pangram labels: AI-Generated | AI-Assisted | Human Written




Attacker & date
Quote




Dragonforce, 2025-07-11
“I’m sure you’ve been following the news. You know that some people have chosen to settle, even after the incident became public. They placed a high value on data privacy. What would be the consequences if you were to handle it differently? It would be a significant news story. We expect a serious proposal from you.”


Dragonforce, 2026-03-08. (Note: Contains curly apostrophes and non-breaking hyphens.)
Hello. In the end, we want to get money from you. We’ve encrypted your files and also downloaded a large number of them to our own servers. We can give you a list of the files we took, along with 1‑3 small samples from that list. We can also decrypt 1‑3 small files that contain non‑critical information to demonstrate that we can recover all of your data. If you’d like, we can do all of that, or we can go straight to the payment request. You see a timer counting down the negotiation period. When it expires, if we don’t receive what we want, we will publish the stolen data publicly and delete the decryption tools, making any recovery of your data completely impossible.


SilentRansomGroup, 2026-03-10
“Our business is built on reputation - if a company were to pay us and, for some reason, we broke our promise, word would spread, negatively impacting our future deals. Clearly, that is not in our interest, as it would lead to a loss of trust from clients.”


SilentRansomGroup, 2026-03-17
“We appreciate your offer, but we are unable to accept it at this time. To clarify, We remain open to negotiation and do not consider our initial figure unchangeable. However, given the critical nature of the situation and the value of the data involved, We must emphasize that We do not believe our current ask is unreasonable.”






Victim messages:
Victims also used AI assistance in writing negotiation messages. Examples:
Pangram labels: AI-Generated | AI-Assisted | Human Written




Victim & date
Quote




Akira victim, 2025-03-10
“After further internal discussions, our limitations remain significant due to bureaucratic approvals and cryptocurrency transfer restrictions. Nevertheless, in the spirit of progressing towards a mutually acceptable resolution, we can increase our offer slightly to $162,000 USD. We kindly ask for your understanding regarding these economic realities and bureaucratic challenges, including the complexity of transferring funds into cryptocurrency. We remain fully committed to reaching an agreement promptly.”


Akira victim, 2025-03-21
“Thank you for the updated offer. This is really appreciated. We understand your effort to reduce the price, but unfortunately, even 135K$ is still far beyond our financial capacity as I already mentioned. Our final and only possible offer remains 50K$, which we can pay quickly. This is not emotional or strategic, it’s a financial and operational constraint. We can’t give you what we don’t have.”


Dragonforce victim, 2026-03-18
"We have completed validation of the data and confirmed your ability to decrypt. At this point, we are moving through the internal authorization process required before any payment can be approved. This step involves multiple parties and cannot be expedited beyond certain requirements. [...] Any early release of the information will disrupt this process and may impact our ability to finalize payment."


SilentRansomGroup victim, 2026-03-27
"We were on the phone with our representative this morning, but they weren't able to provide any new information yet. As soon as we know more, you'll know as well. Please understand that we're not sitting on this, we're actively pressing them for an answer."

title: Have we seen an acceleration in cyberattacks?
text:
Implications and future work
In this blog, we examined several public datasets for evidence of changes in cyberattack activity. Recorded crypto hacks accelerated in 2026, particularly smaller thefts, though the pattern varies across trackers. More ransomware groups posted victims on leak sites, but victim counts did not accelerate, and independently confirmed attacks did not accelerate. We also found evidence of AI-assisted writing in ransomware negotiations.
Our evidence suggests that there might have been an acceleration in crypto attacks in 2026, coinciding with improvements in AI’s cyber capabilities. We note possible confounders that may explain part of the observed increase, including changes in detection and reporting.
Continuing to track AI’s real-world use and impact is important, as Cunningham & Rush (2026) have noted. Researchers should keep on finding, registering, and updating useful data series to inform AI’s real-world impact.
Aside from that, we also see several promising directions for future research in cyber attack acceleration:

Human misuse vs rogue AI agents: Our analysis of ransomware negotiation messages suggests possible AI-assisted drafting, but provides limited evidence about how the underlying attacks were carried out. We suspect these cases are human-directed AI misuse, given links to known ransomware groups. We would like to see future time series analysis that distinguishes human-directed AI use, autonomous agent execution, and rogue behavior in incidents and tracks their prevalence over time.
AI’s impact on cyber offense vs. defense: As AI capabilities improve, both attackers and defenders may become more effective. For instance, AI could help attackers exploit smart contracts and develop ransomware, while helping defenders audit code and detect intrusions. Understanding the relative rates of improvement is essential for assessing AI’s net impact on cybersecurity.
Which models are being used in attacks? Identifying the models involved in real-world cyberattacks, including whether they are open- or closed-weight, would help us understand how different models contribute to emerging cyber risks.
Collect and analyze other datasets: Other sources we considered include npm/PyPI attacks, wallet-drainer phishing, bank transfer fraud, phishing emails, and scam conversations. We encourage timely updates to existing datasets, the development of new datasets, and further analyses as more 2026 data becomes available.

Thanks to Alan Chan, Jake Steckler, and Daniel Paleka for feedback.

title: Have we seen an acceleration in cyberattacks?
text:
Appendix

Appendix A: other crypto hack datasets
We explore six other trackers: SlowMist, Comparitech, CertiK, rekt.news, Web3 Is Going Great, and BlockSec. In each analysis, we make a conclusion about acceleration by comparing each tracker’s average for 2026 Q2-Q3 (for BlockSec, 2026 Q2 only) with two benchmarks: its trend leading up to 2026, and its busiest quarter of 2022-25 (its “old peak”).

SlowMist Hacked: reversal of trend (acceleration), but below its old peak



A list kept by the blockchain security firm SlowMist of every blockchain security incident it finds, including scams and a few incidents in which nothing was stolen.
The acceleration came in March-April 2026.
Caveats: From late 2025, SlowMist more often cited security firms’ monitoring accounts on X, which post when their software spots a likely hack. Such entries rose from about 3 a quarter in 2025 to 25 a quarter in 2026 Q2-Q3, about a third of the roughly 70 extra incidents a quarter; if SlowMist would otherwise have missed these incidents, or if these monitoring accounts used AI to discover attacks, then that part of the rise could reflect discovery rather than more attacks.








Comparitech crypto heists: acceleration, slightly above its old peak



Comparitech compiles its cryptocurrency heist database by searching industry news reports and company announcements worldwide, rather than independently detecting attacks on the blockchain. It includes documented hacks, thefts, flash-loan exploits, and other technical vulnerabilities, but excludes rug pulls, employee theft, and thefts from individuals.
The acceleration came in April 2026.








CertiK incident dashboard: acceleration, above its old peak



CertiK tracks cryptocurrency security incidents through its own on-chain monitoring and investigations, supplemented by publicly available information such as project announcements, social media, and news reports.
The acceleration came in March 2026.
Caveats: CertiK keeps adding incidents to past months (its count for 2026 Q2 across all categories rose from 194 in July to 222 by 18 October), so recent quarters will probably rise further.








rekt.news leaderboard: unclear/no obvious acceleration, below its old peak



Incidents that the crypto news site rekt.news wrote an article about, mostly large DeFi exploits.
No clear acceleration in 2026.
Caveats: editors choose which incidents to cover, almost all of them $1 million or more; its tags rarely say how an attack worked.








Web3 Is Going Great: no acceleration, far below its old peak



One editor’s (Molly White’s) selection of notable crypto events; we count the entries tagged “Hack or scam”.
No acceleration in 2026
Caveats: it is not meant to be complete, and what gets in depends on what the editor finds newsworthy; the tag mixes hacks with scams, phishing and some court cases.








BlockSec security incidents: slight acceleration, slightly above its old peak



BlockSec is a blockchain security firm that sells Phalcon, a system that watches blockchain transactions to detect and block attacks. The page says it lists attacks “with losses of over $100K.”
There is a slight acceleration in 2026.
Caveats: it publishes with a deliberate delay, and its newest entry is from 24 July 2026, so 2026 Q3 is incomplete and left out of the comparison.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
text:
The WSJ article, “China Also Thinks AI Could Kill Us. But First, It Wants to Match the U.S.,” argues that some Chinese researchers see safety work on the most capable AI systems as less urgent because Chinese labs perceive themselves to be trailing U.S. labs.


I see two possible arguments for this view. First, scarcer computing resources mean Chinese labs have less spare compute to devote to safety. Second, less capable models may be involved in fewer safety incidents.


But the second point may not always hold. In this brief note, I argue that China’s AI-safety trajectory need not be a delayed version of America’s, and that safety work in China could make a distinct contribution.


I give three reasons: the incidents may differ, the two countries may disclose them differently, and their governments may respond differently. The relationships shown in the diagrams are hypothetical.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
text:
Baseline model






Figure 1: A baseline model in which safety incidents rise later in China than in the US.






Figure 1 illustrates the baseline model I want to question.


In this model, Chinese models trail US models in capability by a given number of months and are involved in similar safety incidents after a delay.1 As such, China has little independent safety work to do because US researchers will have already identified the problems and developed solutions for the capability levels that Chinese models would eventually reach.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
section: Alternative model: safety incidents need not rise with capability in the same way in the US and China
text:
Alternative model: safety incidents need not rise with capability in the same way in the US and China






Figure 2: Hypothetical: safety incidents rise differently with AI capability in the US and China.






The baseline mental model is misleading.
Firstly, the US and China need not follow the same relationship between capability and safety incidents. Hypothetically, Chinese models could be involved in a particular kind of safety incident at a lower overall capability level than US models. For example, they might escape a sandbox, a restricted computing environment, at a lower capability level because cybersecurity at a Chinese company could be worse. For another example, open-weight models make their numerical parameters available for others to modify. Further training can weaken safety safeguards. Differences in how people use models could also affect which safety incidents occur.


Secondly, the relationship (slope) between safety incidents and capability could also be steeper for one country’s models. A similar increase in capability could accompany a larger increase in safety incidents. A persistent capability gap would therefore not guarantee a persistent gap in incident frequency or severity.


Lastly, even when models pose similar overall risks, the kinds of safety incidents could differ. This example is entirely hypothetical: US models might more often take actions without authorization, while Chinese models might exploit flaws in their reward system rather than complete the intended task. A method that addresses one problem may not address the other.





Evidence and examples


The earliest reports I know of involving US and Chinese models acting beyond their intended sandbox boundaries concern Claude Mythos Preview and ROME, respectively. I also include a later, related example involving Kimi K3. The Chinese models have lower estimated capabilities than Mythos Preview.




US models



Claude Mythos Preview


Reported by Anthropic · April 7, 2026
Anthropic reported that an earlier version of Claude Mythos Preview was put in a secured container and explicitly told to escape and contact the researcher. It developed a multi-step exploit, obtained broader internet access, emailed the researcher, and posted details of the exploit publicly without being asked.
ECI (Epoch Capabilities Index): my rough estimate is about 161.





Chinese models



ROME


Paper first submitted · December 31, 2025
The ROME team reported that, during RL, an AI agent opened a remote-access connection outside its intended environment and used computing resources for cryptocurrency mining. Neither action was requested or necessary for its tasks.
ECI: my rough estimate is about 142.




Kimi K3


Reported by Frontier Security · August 6, 2026
Frontier Security reported that Kimi K3 retrieved a cybersecurity benchmark’s published solution from GitHub instead of solving the task itself. GitHub was reachable through a network allowlist intended for package maintenance, although most websites were blocked. The model was not instructed to escape the sandbox.
ECI: approximately 158 for Kimi K3.





My rough ECI estimates for Mythos Preview and ROME are based mainly on their reported benchmark results and comparisons with models I judged to have similar capabilities.
These cases do not establish when either country first encountered such incidents, or which models are more likely to produce them. Delayed or missing disclosure means earlier incidents may have gone unreported.
I would love to see more rigorous research on how safety incidents relate to capability across companies and countries.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
section: The two countries may disclose safety incidents differently
text:
The two countries may disclose safety incidents differently






Figure 3: Hypothetical differences in public reports of safety incidents.






Public reports give us an incomplete picture of underlying risks. Even if two sets of models were involved in similar safety incidents, differences in evaluation and disclosure could produce different numbers of public reports.


For example, independent evaluators may have different access to labs, and disclosure rules may differ. Figure 3 illustrates how those differences could affect reporting; the direction and size of the gap are hypothetical.





Evidence and examples




Independent evaluation



METR at Anthropic


METR described a researcher spending three weeks testing Anthropic’s monitoring systems in a post published in March 2026. This is an example of an independent evaluator working inside a lab. There is no known embedding of third-party evaluators at Chinese AI companies yet.





Disclosure rules



China’s vulnerability regulations


Chinese vulnerability disclosure rules are more stringent (in terms of CVEs). China’s Regulations on the Management of Security Vulnerabilities in Network Products restrict public disclosure of software and hardware security vulnerabilities (see Article 9). Such rules could affect the public information available about some AI-system vulnerabilities.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
section: Given safety incidents, the Chinese government’s policy responses could differ from the US government’s
text:
Given safety incidents, the Chinese government’s policy responses could differ from the US government’s






Figure 4: Hypothetical policy response differences between the two countries.






Government responses may also differ in two ways: how quickly officials recognize a problem and decide to act, and how quickly an agreed response is carried out.


Recognizing problems: China might have a higher threshold for what is deemed a “problem”.


Policy implementation: China generally acts quickly after a decision.


Figure 4 illustrates one possible outcome. A slowdown threshold is the level of safety incidents at which policymakers decide to intervene. In this scenario, the US starts slowing the rise in incidents after a short delay, at a lower incident level than China. China responds later and slows the rise more sharply, but too late to stay below the hypothetical catastrophe threshold.


Different assumptions could reverse this outcome. If China decided to intervene at a slightly lower incident level and the US took sufficiently long to implement its response, China might in the end have responded more promptly than the US.





Evidence and examples




Policy implementation



Education policy


The central “Double Reduction” policy restricting after-school academic tutoring was issued on July 24, 2021. By December, the Ministry of Education reported that the number of offline academic tutoring institutions had fallen 83.8%, and online institutions 84.1%.




Wuhan lockdown


For Covid-19, Wuhan announced major transport restrictions around 2 a.m. on January 23, 2020, with closures taking effect at 10 a.m. By January 29, all mainland provincial-level jurisdictions had activated the highest emergency-response level, according to the government’s account.





Recognizing problems



Early Covid-19 warnings


Chinese authorities suppressed early COVID-19 warnings. A whistleblower warned about COVID 19 on December 30 but was reprimanded. Wuhan’s transport shutdown began on January 23, more than three weeks after those warnings.




Wenzhou train collision


Before the July 2011 Wenzhou train crash, the Ministry of Railways had prioritized construction speed over safety (e.g. allowing seriously defective train-control equipment into service without field testing). The State Council ordered nationwide high-speed rail safety inspections only after the crash.






In this article, I illustrated several reasons why Chinese contributions to AI safety are important and why Chinese researchers should not be seen as merely following their US counterparts. I want to stress I am not sure about the specifics of the models here, but I do believe the baseline model is too simplistic. I look forward to more work being done to enlighten us about the current situation of AI safety in China.

title: China’s AI-safety trajectory is not necessarily a delayed version of America’s
text:
Footnotes


“Safety incidents” can refer to either the number of incidents or their severity. All relationships and thresholds shown in the diagrams are hypothetical, not measured.↩︎
